IS : 8729 - 1977

Indian Standard
PRINCIPLES OF CONSTRUCTION AND ADJUSTMENT OF VOLUMETRIC GLASSWARE
0. FOREWORD

0.1 This Indian Standard was adopted by the I n d i a n Standards Institution on 27 October 1977, after the draft finalized by the Laboratory Glassware and Related Apparatus Sectional Committee had been approved by the Chemical Division Council. 0.2 This standard is intended to provide general guidelines for formulating specifications for articles of volumetric glassware, and is based on draft ISO Standard 384 'Principles of construction and adjustment of volumetric glassware', issued by the International Organization for Standardization ( ISO ). 0.3 In this standard important information regarding basis of adjustment, volumetric accuracy, construction, graduation, etc, of volumetric glassware has been provided. In addition to this, appendices covering limits of volumetric error in relation to capacity and diameter at the meniscus and interrelation between standard deviation, limit of volumetric error, line thickness and also line spacing on articles having a scale, have also been included with suitable examples to explain their application in the adjustment of volumetric glassware.

1. SCOPE 1.1 This standard lays down the principles of construction and adjust ment of volumetric glassware. 2. BASIS OF ADJUSTMENT 2.1 Unit of Volume -- The unit of volume shall be the cubic centimetre ( cm 3 ) or, in special cases, the cubic decimetre ( dm 3 ) or cubic millimetre 3 ( mm ).
NOTE -- The term millilitre ( ml ) is commonly used as a special name for the cubic centimetre ( c m 3 ) and similarly, the litre (1) for the cubic decimetre ( dm 3 ) and the microlitre ( l ) for the cubic millimetre ( m m 3 ), in accordance with the International System of Units ( SI ).

3

IS : 8729 - 1977 2.2 Reference Temperature -- The standard reference temperature, that is, the temperature at which the article of volumetric glassware is intended to contain or deliver its nominal volume (nominal capacity), shall be 27�C. 3. VOLUMETRIC ACCURACY 3.1 In a specification where two classes of accuracy are prescribed, the higher grade shall be designated 'Class A', and the lower grade shall be designated 'Class B'. 3.2 Limits of volumetric error shall be specified for each type of article having regard to the method and purpose of use and the class of accuracy. 3.3 The numerical values of limits of volumetric error for articles of volumetric glassware for general purposes shall be chosen from the series: 10, 12, 15, 20, 25, 30, 40, 50, 60, 80 or a suitable decimal multiple thereof.
N O T E -- This is the R 10 series ( second rounding ) of preferred numbers and has been adopted because decimal sub-multiples of some of the unrounded numbers, for example, 13.5, would appear to imply a degree of precision which is not intended and which could not be measured in practice.

3.4 The limits of volumetric error specified for a series of sizes of an article shall provide a reasonably uniform progression in relation to capacity when plotted on a logarithmic graph as shown in Appendix A. Such a graph should be included as an annexure to all specifications in which a series of 3 or more sizes of an article is specified. 3.5 Where two classes of accuracy are specified, the limits of volumetric error permitted for Class B shall in general be approximately twice those permitted for Class A. 3.6 For all articles having a scale, the maximum permitted volumetric error for either class of accuracy shall not exceed the volume equivalent of the smallest scale division. 3.7 Where two classes of accuracy are specified, the Class A limit of volumetric error specified for any article shall not be smaller than that calculated from the maximum permitted diameter at the relevant graduation line by the formula detailed in Appendix B. The corresponding Class B limit shall be derived in accordance with 3.5.
N O T E -- Where only one class of accuracy is specified, the limit of volumetric error specified for any article shall be similarly determined, on the basis of a preliminary decision as to whether Class A or Class B accuracy is appropriate to the article in question. A nomograph, plotted on a logarithmic scale as shown in Appendix B, should be ncluded as an appendix to all specifications for articles of volumetric glassware.

4

IS : 8729 - 1977 3.8 The limit of volumetric error specified for any article adjusted for delivery shall also not be less than four times the standard deviation, ( RMS ) determined experimentally by an experienced operator from a series of at least 20 replicable determinations of delivered capacity on the same article, carried out strictly in accordance with the method specified for that article. 4. METHODS OF VERIFICATION AND USE 4.1 The method of verification shall be clearly specified for each article of volumetric glassware [ see Indian Standard 'Method of verification and tables for calibration of volumetric glassware' ( under preparation ) ]. 4.2 Any difference between the method of verification and the method of use shall be clearly indicated. 4.3 Delivery times and, where applicable, waiting times for all articles intended for delivery of a liquid shall be specified. 4.4 Setting of the meniscus shall be performed by one of the two methods detailed below. Wherever practicable, the meniscus should descend to the position of setting: a) The meniscus is set so that the plane of the upper edge of the graduation line is horizontally tangential to the lowest point of the meniscus, the line of sight being in the same plane. In the case of a mercury meniscus, however, the highest point of the meniscus is set to the lower edge of the graduation line. b) The meniscus is set so that the plane of the centre of the graduation line is horizontally tangential to the lowest point of the meniscus. The eye is raised towards the plane and observes the front and back portions of the line apparently meeting the lowest point simultaneously. In the case of mercury meniscus, the eye is lowered towards the plane of the centre of the graduation line.
N O T E -- The difference between meniscus positions resulting from the alternative methods of adjustment is the volume equivalent of one half the thickness of the graduation line. In the case of articles where the capacity is read as the difference between two meniscus readings ( for example, on a burette ) no error results if the article is graduated using one method of adjustment and is later used by the other method. Even in the most unfavourable cases of single mark articles ( for example, large flasks ), when working to the highest attainable accuracy, the difference between the two methods of adjustment is unlikely to exceed 30 percent of the Class A limit of error and a correction can be calculated where necessary.

4.5 When the article is used with opaque wetting liquids, the horizontal line of sight shall be taken through the upper edge of the meniscus, and where necessary, an appropriate correction shall be applied.
5

IS : 8729 - 1977 5. CONSTRUCTION 5.1 Materials -- Volumetric glassware shall be constructed of glass of suitable chemical and thermal properties, shall be as free as possible from visible defects and reasonably free from internal stress. 5.2 Shape -- All articles shall be of a shape which will facilitate emptying and drainage and shall preferably be of circular cross section. 5.3 Capacity 5.3.1 The numerical values of capacity of articles of volumetric glassware for general purposes shall preferably be chosen from the series: 10, 20, 25, 50 or a decimal multiple or submultiple thereof. 5.3.2 The numerical value of the volume equivalents of the smallest division of an article having a scale shall be chosen from the series: 1, 2, 5 or a decimal multiple or submultiple thereof. 5.3.3 In the case of a special purpose article of volumetric glassware which is to be adjusted for direct reading of capacity when used with a specific liquid other than water, the specification shall also indicate the corresponding capacity when pure water is used so that the latter may be used for verification.
N O T E -- In case of some special purpose volumetric glassware meant to read percentages directly the corresponding volume shall be specified for verification.

5.4 Stability -- Vessels provided with a flat base shall stand firmly thereon without rocking when placed on a level surface and, unless specified otherwise, the axis of the graduated portion of the vessel shall be vertical. Wherever practicable, vessels shall not topple when placed empty on a surface inclined at an angle to the horizontal to be specified for each item. 5.4.1 Vessels provided with a base which is not circular shall meet this requirement in all directions. 5.5 Delivery Jets 5.5.1 Delivery jets shall be strongly constructed with a smooth and gradual taper without any sudden constriction at the orifice.
N O T E -- The reason for not permitting a sudden construction at the orifice is that such a shape could conceal the fact that the jet had been damaged, cut back and refired. Following such treatment the volume delivered by the article could have been altered beyond the specified limits of volumetric error without any visible evidence of the fact.

6

IS : 8729 - 1977 5.5.2 The end of the jet shall be finished by one of the methods listed below in order of preference: a) Smoothly ground square with the axis, slightly bevelled on the outside and fire-polished. b) Smoothly ground square with the axis and slightly bevelled on the outside. c) Cut square with the axis and fire-polished.
N O T E -- A fire-polished finish reduces the danger of chipping in use, but should not result in construction as indicated in 5.5.1 , or in undue stress.

5.5.3 The jet shall form an integral part of an article intended for Class A and may form an integral part of an article intended for Class B. 5.6 Stoppers 5.6.1 Glass stoppers shall preferably be ground so as to be interchangeable, in which case the ground portions shall comply with the provisions of IS : 5165-1969*. If individually fitted, they shall be well-ground so as to prevent leakage, preferably with a taper approximating 1 : 1 0 . 5.6.2 Stoppers of a suitably inert plastics material may be permitted as an alternative to glass. In such cases, the glass socket into which the stopper fits shall preferably comply with the provisions of IS : 5165-1969*. 5.7 Stopcocks or Similar Devices 5.7.1 Stopcocks and similar devices shall be designed to permit smooth and precise control of outflow and to prevent a rate of leakage greater than that allowed in the specification for the article. 5.7.2 Stopcocks and similar devices shall be made from glass or from suitable inert plastics material. 5.7.3 All-glass stopcocks shall have the key and barrel finely ground preferably to a taper of 1 : 10 and shall comply with IS : 5165-1969*. 5.7.4 Glass stopcock barrels to receive plastics keys shall be polished internally. 5.7.5 Stopcock components may be fitted with suitable retaining devices. 6. LINEAR DIMENSIONS 6.1 Linear dimensional requirements shall be specified in millimetres for all articles of volumetric glassware in such a way as to ensure that: a) the article is convenient and satisfactory for its intended use;
*Specification for interchangeable conical ground-glass joints.

7

IS : 8729 - 1977 b) in a series of sizes of an article unnecessary inconsistencies in shape a n d proportions are avoided; c) a limitation is placed on t h e m a x i m u m internal diameter at the g r a d u a t i o n line or lines ( see 3.7 a n d A p p e n d i x B ). This limitation m a y be a direct limitation on diameter or an indirect one by a m i n i m u m limitation on scale length; d) t h e stability r e q u i r e m e n t s of 5.4 can be achieved; a n d e) the requirement for spacing of g r a d u a t i o n lines specified in 8.1.2 is achieved.
N O T E -- The stability requirement is controlled by the angle of displacement from the vertical at which the centre of gravity comes vertically above the edge of the base. The height of the centre of gravity is not only a function ot the specified dimensions but it is also affected by the distribution of mass in the parts of the article. It is, however, important to ensure that the specified dimensions do not make it difficult or impossible to achieve the required stability.

6.2 Dimensional r e q u i r e m e n t s shall not be necessary to achieve the aims listed in 6.1.

more restrictive t h a n is

6.3 In order to permit m a x i m u m freedom in manufacture within t h e restrictions imposed by 6.1 , dimensions m a y be divided into two categories of i m p o r t a n c e a n d classified as 'essential dimensions' a n d ' g u i d a n c e dimensions'. 6.4 In a specification where these two categories of dimensions are used, t h e r e q u i r e m e n t s of 6.1 (c) a n d 6.1 (e) shall be included as essential dimensions. 6.5 T h e requirements of 6.1 (b) are in m a n y cases sufficiently ensured by guidance dimensions. 6.6 Essential dimensions shall be expressed in one of t h e following ways, whichever is the most suitable or convenient: a) A m e d i a n figure with � tolerance; b) A m a x i m u m a n d a m i n i m u m figure; a n d c) A m a x i m u m or a m i n i m u m figure, if the other limit is u n i m p o r t a n t or is controlled by other factors in the specification.
N O T E -- The choice between 6.6 (a) and 6.6 (b) will often be guided by economy or simplicity of figures and sometimes by the avoidance of an implication of greater precision than is intended.

6.7 A d u a l limitation on dimensional tolerances shall be avoided wherever possible, for example, if an overall length is limited by the m e t h o d s shown in 6.6 (a) or 6.6 (b) a n d there are two or more additive components of this length to be specified, t h e n either t h e tolerance on overall length should be sufficient to a c c o m m o d a t e the additive tolerance of all the components, or the least i m p o r t a n t component should be left u n d i m e n sioned so t h a t it is controlled only by the difference between overall length a n d the total of the other components.

8

IS : 8729 - 1977 6.8 Guidance dimensions shall be expressed as median figures without tolerances or as minima or maxima. If both limits are considered necessary, then the dimensions in question shall be classed as an essential dimension. 7. GRADUATION LINES 7.1 Graduation lines shall be clean, permanent lines of uniform thickness. 7.2 Maximum thickness of graduation lines shall be specified appropriate to the particular article and its class of accuracy. This thickness shall not exceed one half of the linear equivalent of the limit of volumetric error ( see Appendix C ). 7.3 On articles having a scale, the specified maximum thickness of lines shall not exceed one quarter of the minimum distance between centres of adjacent lines ( see Appendix C ). 7.4 All graduation lines shall lie in planes at right angles to the longitudinal axis of the graduated portion of the article. On articles provided with a flat base, the graduation lines shall lie in planes parallel to the base. 7.5 In general, graduation lines shall be confined to cylindrical portions of cross section of an article and should preferably be situated not less than 10 mm from any change in diameter. In special circumstances, preferably for Class B articles only, graduation lines may be provided on a parallel side portion of non-circular cross section or on a conical or tapered portion of the article. 7.6 On articles not having a scale, all graduation lines shall extend completely round the circumference of the article, except for a gap, not exceeding 10 percent of the circumference, which may be permitted. In the case of an article which is restricted as to the normal direction of viewing in use, this gap shall be either at the right or left to the normal direction of view. 8. SCALES 8.1 Spacing of Graduation Lines 8.1.1 There shall be no evident irregularity in the spacing of graduation lines ( except in special cases where the scale is on a conical or tapered portion of the article and a change of subdivision takes place ). 8.1.2 The minimum distance between the centres of adjacent graduation lines shall be not less, in relation to diameter, than that calculated from the formula: ( 0.8 + 0.02 D ) mm, where D is the maximum permitted internal diameter of the tube in millimetres ( see also Appendix C ).
9

IS : 8729 - 1977 8.2 Length of Graduation Lines (See Fig. 1) -- On articles of circular cross section having a scale, the length of the graduation lines shall be varied so as to be clearly distinguishable and shall be in accordance with the provisions of 8.2.1, 8.2.2 and 8.2.3.
N O T E -- In special cases where scales are required on non-circular cross section or conical or tapered portions of an article the requirements of 8.2.3 shall be appropriately modified.

8.2.1 Graduation Lines -- Pattern I ( See Fig. 1A ): a) The length of the short lines shall be approximately but not less than 50 percent of the circumference of the article; b) The length of the medium lines shall be approximately 65 percent of the circumference of the article. The lines shall extend symmetrically at each end beyond the ends of the short lines; and c) The long lines shall extend completely round the circumference of the article, except for a gap not exceeding 10 percent of the circumference, which may be permitted ( see 7.6 ). 8.2.2 Graduation Lines -- Pattern II ( See Fig. 1B ): a) The length of the short lines shall be not less than 10 percent and not more than 20 percent of the circumference; b) The length of the medium lines shall be approximately 1.5 times the length of the short lines. The lines shall extend symmetrically at each end beyond the ends of the short lines; and c) The long lines shall extend completely round the circumference of the article, except for a gap, not exceeding 10 percent of the circumference, which may be permitted ( see 7.6 ). 8.2.3 Graduation Lines -- Pattern III ( See Fig. 1C ) : a) The length of the short lines shall not be less than 10 percent and not more than 20 percent of the circumference; b) The length of the medium lines shall be approximately 1.5 times the length of the short lines. The lines shall extend symmetrically at each end beyond the ends of the short lines; and c) The long lines shall be not less than twice the length of the short lines and they shall extend symmetrically at each end beyond the ends of the short and medium lines. 8.3 Sequence of Graduation Lines ( See Fig. 1 ) 8.3.1 On articles in which the volume equivalent of the smallest scale division is 1 ml or a decimal multiple or submultiple thereof: a) Every tenth graduation line shall be a long line, 10

IS : 8729 - 1977 b) There shall be one medium line midway between two consecutive long lines, and c) There shall be four short lines between consecutive medium and long lines. 8.3.2 On articles in which the volume equivalent of the smallest scale division is 2 ml or a decimal multiple or submultiple thereof: a) Every fifth graduation lines shall be a long line, and b) There shall be four short lines between two consecutive long lines. 8.3.3 On articles in which the volume equivalent of the smallest scale division is 5 ml or a decimal multiple or submultiple thereof: a) Every tenth graduation line shall be a long line, b) There shall be four medium lines equally spaced between two consecutive long lines, and c) There shall be one short line between two consecutive medium lines or between consecutive medium and long lines. 8.4 Position of Graduation Lines ( See Fig. 2 ) 8.4.1 On articles graduated according to Pattern I with vertical scales in accordance with 8.2.1 the ends of the short graduation lines shall lie on an imaginary vertical line down the centre of the front of the article, the lines themselves extending preferably to the left when the article is viewed from the front in the position of normal use. 8.4.2 On articles graduated according to Pattern II or III, with vertical scales in accordance with 8.2.2 or 8.2.3 the mid-points of the short and medium graduation lines shall lie on an imaginary vertical line down the centre of the front of the article when the article is viewed from the front in the position of normal use. 9. FIGURING OF GRADUATION LINES 9.1 On articles with one graduation line, the number representing nomimal capacity may be included with other inscriptions and need not be adjacent to the graduation line. 9.2 On articles having two or three graduation lines, the numbers representing nominal capacity need not be adjacent to the lines to which they relate, if some other more suitable method of identification is used [ for example, as covered in 11.1(d) ]. 9.3 On articles having one principal graduation line and a small number of subsidiary lines, the number representing the principal capacity may be included with other inscription as in 9.1 provided that the subsidiary graduation lines are suitably identified. 11

IS : 8729 - 1977

FIG. 1

LENGTH AND SEQUENCE OF GRADUATION LINES

POSITION OF GRADUATION LINES

12

IS : 8729 - 1977 9.4 On articles having a scale: a) the scale shall be so figured as to enable the value corresponding to each graduation line to be readily identified, b) the scale shall normally have only one set of figures, c) at least every tenth line shall be figured, and d) figures shall be confined to long graduation lines and shall be placed immediately above the line and slightly to the right of the adjacent shorter graduation lines.
N O T E -- Where long lines complying with 8.2.2 are used ( that is, not extending completely round the article ), an alternative scheme of figuring may be permitted, in which the figure is placed slightly to the right of the end of the long line in such a way that an extension of the line would bisect it. Where it is necessary, in special cases, to use a number relating to a medium or short graduation line, the number shall be placed slightly to the right of the end of the line in such a way that an extension of the line would bisect it.

10. VISIBILITY OF GRADUATION LINES, FIGURES AND INSCRIPTIONS 10.1 All figures and inscriptions shall be of such size and form as to be clearly legible under normal conditions of use. 10.2 All graduation lines, figures and inscriptions shall be clearly visible and permanent. 11. INSCRIPTIONS 11.1 The following inscriptions shall be permanently marked on each article: a) A number indicating the nominal capacity ( except for articles with graduation lines figured to indicate capacity ); b) The symbol 'cm 3 ' or the symbol 'ml' to indicate the unit of volume in terms of which the article is graduated ( see Note under 2.1 ); c) The inscription '27�C' to indicate the standard reference temperature; d) The letters 'In' to indicate that the article has been adjusted to contain its indicated capacity or the letters 'Ex' to indicate that the article has been adjusted to deliver its indicated capacity. Where the article has graduation lines intended to indicate both content and delivery, the letters shall be close to the line to which they refer; e) The inscription 'A' or 'B' to indicate the class of accuracy to which the article is intended to belong; and f) The maker's or vendor's name orrecognized trade-mark. 11.1.1 On articles intended for use with a specified waiting time, the waiting time shall be inscribed, for example, Ex + 15s. 13

IS : 8729 - 1977 11.2 The following additional inscriptions shall be marked on Class A articles intended for official verification or certification. They shall preferably be marked on all Class A articles and may also be used, if desired, on Class B articles: a) An identification number. The same numbers shall be marked on the handles of stopcocks, if required, and also on stoppers which are not interchangeable. If interchangeable glass stoppers are provided then the stopper and neck shall be marked with the joint size designation in accordance with IS : 5165-1969*; b) On articles intended for delivery through a jet, the time in seconds for unrestricted delivery of the contents, using pure water; c) In the case of an article of volumetric glassware which has been specially adjusted for direct reading of capacity when used with a specific liquid other than water, the name or chemical formula of the liquid in question; and d) The limit of volumetric error, valid for the article, that is, � ... ml. 11.3 The following inscriptions shall also be marked on articles to which they apply: a) In the case of an article made from glass having co-efficient of cubical thermal expansion outside the range 25 � 10 -6 /�C to 30 � 10-6/�C (that is outside the range of the usual types of sodalime glass ), an indication to this effect, so that for certification purposes the appropriate correction table may be selected.
N O T E -- The requirement of this clause may be met by the manufacturer's name or trade-mark if the coefficient of thermal expansion is published in the corresponding catalogues.

b) In the case of pipettes adjusted for delivery to include the last drop being blown out of the jet, the word BLOWOUT and/or a white enamelled, ( or etched or sandblasted ) band, 3 to 5 mm. wide, approximately 15 to 20 mm from the top of suction tube.

*Specification for interchangeable conical ground-glass joints.

APPENDIX ( Clause 3.4 )

A

LIMIT OF VOLUMETRIC ERROR IN RELATION TO CAPACITY A-0. GENERAL A-0.1 This standard prescribes a requirement that limits of volumetric error for each size of an article, when a series of 3 or more sizes are specified, shall be chosen so as to provide a reasonably uniform progression in relation to the capacities of the article. The attainment of this requirement can most conveniently be checked by means of a graph of the form shown in Fig. 3.

FIG. 3 GRAPH SHOWING RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN LIMIT OF CLASS A VOLUMETRIC ERROR AND NOMINAL CAPACITY

15

IS : 8729 - 1977 A-1. INTERPRETATION A-1.1 The logarithmic decades on this graph can be scaled in tenths, units, tens, etc, as appropriate to the series of capacities of the article in question and their proposed limits of volumetric error. The decade rulings shown include heavy lines for the preferred values of errors listed in 3.3 and of capacities listed in 5.3.1. Thin line rulings are shown for other capacities which may be required for special purposes. A-1.2 The three lines shown on the graph, by way of example, illustrate features as follows. A-1.2.1 Line 1 -- This refers to a series of sizes in which the limits of error are directly proportional to capacity, that is, errors which increase decade by decade with capacity. A proportion of that order of magnitude is likely to be applicable to a series of sizes of an article in which capacity and diameter are variables but the length is approximately constant throughout the range of sizes, for example, graduated pipettes. A-1.2.1.1 The slope of this line is 1 in 1 or 45� to the base line, and in the example shown, would represent a limit of volumetric error constant at 2 percent ( or 0.2 percent or 0.02 percent according to the decade scale ) of capacity throughout the range of sizes. A-1.2.1.2 The broken lines of similar slope shown as lines 1a and 1b indicate a similar proportional relationship between error and capacity but of different magnitudes corresponding to 1 percent ( or 0.1 percent, etc ) and 5 percent ( or 0.5 percent, etc ) respectively. A-1.2.1.3 The 'x' point shown near line (1) illustrates less satisfactory limits of error which would have resulted if the 2 and 2.5 sizes ( in either decade ) had been allotted the same limits of error. A-1.2.2 Line 2 -- This refers to a series of sizes in which the limits of error increase by one decade for two decades increase in capacity. A proportion of this order of magnitude is likely to be applicable to one-mark articles in which all three linear dimensions increase proportionately with increase of capacity, for example, one-mark pipettes or flasks. A-1.2.2.1 The slope of this line is 1 in 2 or approximately 26� 30' to the base line. A series of articles to which a graph with a slope of anything less than 45� applies will provide increasing precision with increasing capacity. A-1.2.2.2 In such cases many of the plotted points will not lie exactly on a straight line. When a specification is being drafted, the aim should be to choose the line which provides the best possible fit to the plotted points and then to check that, for each capacity, the nearest available preferred limit of error has been selected. In the example illustrated, 16

IS : 8729 - 1977 two alternative errors have been shown against capacity 5 in each decade, in each case the one marked with a circle being preferable to the alternative marked. A-1.2.3 Line 3 -- This illustrates the third possibility which may be required in certain cases where very small capacities are included in a series of sizes. The upper section is a straight line with an angle of slope between 26� 30' and 45� as described in the preceding clause, but the lower continuation of the line is a curve of reducing angle of slope which, in limiting cases, may become horizontal at the extreme end. A-1.2.3.1 There are two potential causes for this reduction in angle of slope on very small articles, namely: a) it may be impracticable to reduce the diameter at the graduated line sufficiently to accommodate a smaller limit of error within the limitation of 3.7, for example, one-mark flasks below about 10 ml capacity are inconvenient if the neck is of such a small diameter that the flask cannot be readily filled or emptied, or will not permit the entry of pipette of suitable capacity; and b) in the case of small articles intended for delivery, for example, pipettes of capacity smaller than about 0.5 ml, the standard deviation requirements of 3.8 may be more restrictive than the diameter limitation of 3.7 in preventing the use of smaller limits of error. A-2. RECOMMENDATIONS A-2.1 The graph shown as an example in this appendix is designed for explanatory purposes and includes two complete logarithmic decades on each of the axes. The numerals shown on these decades are only logarithmic and do not indicate any orders of magnitude. A-2.2 The graph as recommended in 3.4 to be included in appropriate standards should be fully figured so as to give direct reading for capacities and limits of error. It should preferably include only the ranges of capacity and limits of error required in the individual specification to which it applies and should be drawn to the largest scale which can be accommodated within the size of the page, that is, a limit width of 150 mm. A-2.3 In the case of specifications which include two classes of accuracy, it should be sufficient for the graph to show only the Class A limits of error unless, in a special case, ratio of errors different from that required by 3.5 has been adopted.

APPENDIX

[ Clauses 3.7 and 6.1 (c) ]
LIMIT OF VOLUMETRIC ERROR IN RELATION TO DIAMETER AT THE MENISCUS B-0. GENERAL B-0.1 This standard specifies a requirement that the limit of volumetric error specified for any article shall not be less than that calculated for the maximum permitted diameter by means of a formula. The reason for this requirement is to ensure that the intended precision of the article can be readily attained under normal conditions of use, that is, that a volume equal to the limit of volumetric error should occupy a readily visible length of tube of the maximum diameter allowed. B-1. THE FORMULA B-1.1 The following symbols are used in deriving the formula: V = the limit of volumetric error in microlitres, D = the internal diameter in millimetres of the tube at the meniscus, and L = the linear equivalent of V in millimetres of tube of diameter D occupied by a volume equal to V. L can be considered to be made up of two components, namely, a) a basic minimum of 0.4 mm which is the lowest limit, even on tubes of very small diameter, which has proved to be satisfactory in normal use and practicable for economic routine manufacture; and b) an additional allowance for potential parallax errors in read ing, which will be related to the diameter, and for which the symbol '  ' is used. B-1.1.1 The value for this parallax component can be derived as follows: a) If  is the angle between the operator's sight-line to the meniscus, and the horizontal plane tangential to the meniscus, then:

18

IS : 8729 - 1977 where p = error in reading in millimetres; d = distance of operator's eye from the scale in millimetres; H = distance of operator's eye above or below the horizontal plane tangential to the meniscus in millimetres; and D = diameter of tube, neck of column which carries the scale in millimetres. b) If H = 5 mm, and d = 200 mm then  = cover the extreme range of diameters

c) If D = 1 mm then p = 0.0125 mm = 0.0125 D; and again, if D = 100 mm then p = 1.0 mm = 0.0100 D So without significant error a constant figure of 0.01 D can be substituted.
N O T E -- It should be noted that this formula tends to exaggerate the potential parallax error on a meniscus greater than about 25 mm diameter. In such a case the flat centre portion of the meniscus helps to minimize parallax error but the effect does not significantly affect this formula.

B-1.1.3 Again without significant error -- can be rounded to 0.8 and the result can be divided by 1 000 to convert to cm .

B-3. RECOMMENDATIONS B-3.1 Clause 3.7 of this standard includes a requirement that a nomo graph of this pattern should be included as an appendix to each standard for article of volumetric glassware: a) to indicate the basis on which the standard has been prepared; 21

IS : 8729 - 1977 b) to place the data on record so that future revisions of the standard, or new standards for allied articles, can be facilitated and adequately correlated; and c) to assist in the preparation of standards, particularly in those cases where additional sizes not included in the standard are required. B-3.2 The nomograph used for any particular standard should include only the ranges of diameter and limit of error required for the articles to which it applies and should also include the relevant section of the limit curve on which the limit of error lines terminate.

APPENDIX C ( Clauses 7.2, 7.3 and 8.1.2 )
INTERRELATION BETWEEN STANDARD DEVIATION, LIMIT OF VOLUMETRIC ERROR AND LINE THICKNESS ( ALSO LINE SPACING ON ARTICLES HAVING A SCALE ) C-0. GENERAL C-0.1 In this standard several of the requirements are related to one another in a logical manner so as to facilitate the most reliable and convenient use of the article to the intended degree of accuracy. Appendix B explains the derivation of a formula relating tube diameter to linear equivalent L and thus to limit of volumetric error V. C-1. DERIVATION OF RELATIONSHIP C-1.1 Clause 7.2 places a limit on the thickness of graduation line of an article not having a scale, this limit being not greater than one half the linear equivalent L of the volumetric error. C-1.2 Clause 3.6 requires that the linear equivalent should not exceed one division of scale. For articles for which two classes of accuracy are specified, this in effect limits the volumetric error for Class A to one half the scale division. C-1.3 Clause 8.1.2 specifies the minimum spacing of the smallest scale division as: ( 0.8 + 0.02 D ) mm that is, twice as great as L. 22

IS : 8729 - 1977 C-1.4 Clause 7.3 specifies a maximum thickness of line as one quarter of the line spacing and clause 3.8 that the limit of volumetric error shall not be less than four times the standard deviation. C-1.5 In terms of linear measurement along the tube or scale, these factors can thus be tabulated as follows: Standard deviation Line thickness L for Class A Line spacing 1 2 maximum 4 maximum 8 minimum
